title: Building an ML Model with Scikit-learn
summary: Build a complete, working ML pipeline end-to-end: load data, split it, train a model, and evaluate it correctly.

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

In class you watched the whole machine-learning pipeline run on one dataset. Now you build it yourself, start to finish, on a different one: `plants.csv` holds 50 house plants with how much water each got per week, its hours of sunlight per day, how many times a month it was fed, and whether it stayed healthy (yes or no). The label is a category, so this is a classification task. You will load the file with pandas, pick the features and the label, split into train and test sets, train a classifier, and measure its accuracy on rows it has never seen. Every stage gets a short comment saying what it does, because a pipeline you can explain is a pipeline you can trust.

lab.title: Pipeline: will the plant stay healthy?
lab.objective: Build the full load -> features/label -> split -> fit -> predict -> evaluate pipeline on plants.csv and report train and test accuracy.
lab.instructions:
The file plants.csv has 50 rows and the columns water_ml, sunlight_hours, fertiliser_per_month and healthy (the words yes or no). Build the pipeline in this order and put a one-line comment above each stage saying what it does.

1. Load: df = pd.read_csv("plants.csv"). Print Rows: 50 using len(df).
2. Features and label: X = df[["water_ml", "sunlight_hours", "fertiliser_per_month"]] and y = df["healthy"]. Keep the labels as the words yes and no; scikit-learn accepts text labels.
3. Split: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0). Print Train rows: 40 and Test rows: 10.
4. Model: the label is a category, so use a classifier: model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0) or model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000). Then model.fit(X_train, y_train).
5. Evaluate: predictions = model.predict(X_test) and accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions). Also compute train_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train)). Print Train accuracy: <value> and then Test accuracy: <value>, each rounded to 2 decimals.

If the train accuracy is much higher than the test accuracy, you are looking at the overfitting signature from the last lecture. That is fine here; just notice it.
lab.constraints: Read the data from plants.csv. Use test_size=0.2 and random_state=0 in the split, and random_state=0 if you use a decision tree. Keep the names df, X, y, X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, model, predictions, accuracy and train_accuracy. Keep the labels as the words yes and no. No input().

lab.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Stage 1 - Load: read the CSV into a DataFrame so we can work with columns
df = pd.read_csv("plants.csv")
print("Rows:", len(df))

# Stage 2 - Features and label: X is what the model sees, y is what it must predict
X = df[["water_ml", "sunlight_hours", "fertiliser_per_month"]]
y = df["healthy"]

# Stage 3 - Split: keep 20% of rows aside so we can test on data the model never saw
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
print("Train rows:", len(X_train))
print("Test rows:", len(X_test))

# Stage 4 - Model: the label is a category, so a classifier; fit learns from the training rows
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Stage 5 - Evaluate: accuracy on the test rows is the honest score; train accuracy shows overfitting
predictions = model.predict(X_test)
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
train_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train))
print(f"Train accuracy: {train_accuracy:.2f}")
print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
